triage.name: Cough
triage.reason: Extremely common presenting symptom with a broad differential that students must narrow by history, exam and targeted testing.

demographics: Adults presenting to primary care with a new cough most often have an acute viral upper respiratory infection
Adults with cough lasting more than 8 weeks are more often female
Children and older adults are more likely to have a lower respiratory tract infection rather than a simple cold

risk_factors.text: Recent contact with someone who has a cold or flu
Cigarette smoking or living with a smoker
Working or living in a dusty or moldy environment

family_history: Asthma or atopy in first-degree relatives
social_history: Secondhand smoke exposure at home or work
Recent travel or crowded living conditions
exposures: Household contacts with a recent cold or flu

chief_complaints.text: I've been coughing for a few days
My throat is scratchy and I keep coughing
I cough up phlegm in the morning

hpi.onset: Sudden or gradual, often starting a few days after a sore throat or runny nose
hpi.duration: Acute cough usually less than 3 weeks; chronic cough more than 8 weeks
hpi.progression: Often worst in the first few days and slowly improving; a dry cough can linger for weeks after other cold symptoms resolve
hpi.quality: Dry and hacking, or wet and productive of clear to yellow sputum
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; often worse at night and disruptive to sleep
hpi.timing: Intermittent, triggered by talking, cold air, or lying down

associated_symptoms.text: Heartburn or sour taste in the mouth

pertinent_negatives: Severe shortness of breath at rest
Long history of smoking with changing cough character

positives.text: Cough worse after meals or when lying down
Symptoms worse around pets or pollen

negatives: Swelling of the lips or tongue

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children cannot describe their cough well; parents report noisy breathing, poor feeding, or a barking cough at night. Cough medicines are not recommended under age 4.
May have a blunted fever response and a weaker cough reflex, so pneumonia can present with confusion or falls rather than prominent cough.
Cough is often from a viral illness or reflux, but shortness of breath and leg swelling should raise concern for a clot.
Can develop severe or unusual lung infections with minimal symptoms and a normal chest exam.

general.mild: Well-appearing, speaking in full sentences, no distress
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, occasional cough interrupting speech, no respiratory distress
general.severe: Ill-appearing, coughing frequently, mild tachypnea or use of accessory muscles
general.critical: Toxic or exhausted, unable to speak in full sentences, marked respiratory distress or altered mental status

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields, anterior and posterior, with the patient breathing deeply through the mouth
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lung bases posteriorly
findings.finding: Inspiratory crackles or rales

findings.maneuver: Auscultate during quiet and forced expiration
findings.finding: Diffuse expiratory wheezing

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the large airways
findings.finding: Coarse rhonchi that clear with coughing

findings.maneuver: Listen to the expiratory phase during tidal breathing
findings.finding: Prolonged expiratory phase suggesting airflow obstruction

findings.maneuver: Percuss the posterior lung fields
findings.finding: Focal dullness suggesting consolidation or effusion

findings.maneuver: Assess tactile fremitus with the ulnar surface of the hands while the patient speaks
findings.finding: Increased tactile fremitus over a consolidated area

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to say 'E' while auscultating over the area of concern
findings.finding: E-to-A change suggesting consolidation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a light and tongue blade
findings.finding: Mild erythema without exudate, no asymmetry or swelling

findings.maneuver: Inspect the posterior pharynx
findings.finding: Visible post-nasal drip or cobblestoning of the posterior pharynx

findings.maneuver: Otoscopic exam of both tympanic membranes
findings.finding: Clear, mobile tympanic membranes without effusion or erythema

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal mucosa and turbinates
findings.finding: Mild mucosal edema or clear discharge without purulence or polyps

findings.maneuver: Palpate the neck for lymphadenopathy and inspect for tracheal deviation
findings.finding: No significant lymphadenopathy, trachea midline

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the standard valve areas
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops

findings.maneuver: Assess jugular venous pressure with the patient at 30–45 degrees
findings.finding: JVP not elevated

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower extremities for edema and assess capillary refill
findings.finding: No peripheral edema, warm extremities

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of alertness
findings.finding: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's breathing at rest
findings.finding: Use of accessory muscles of respiration or intercostal retractions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, oral mucosa, and nail beds
findings.finding: Central or peripheral cyanosis

differential.name: Community-acquired pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Cough with fever and chest symptoms is the classic presentation of a lower respiratory tract infection
differential.trigger: Fever, tachypnea, focal crackles, or hypoxemia in a patient with cough

history: Cough worsening rather than improving over days
exam: Focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds
imaging: Focal airspace opacity or consolidation on chest radiograph

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Cough and shortness of breath can be the presenting symptom of a clot in the lungs
differential.trigger: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, or hypoxemia without another clear explanation

history: Recent surgery, immobilization, or long travel
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
Unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness
labs: Hypoxemia with a normal chest radiograph
imaging: Filling defect on CT pulmonary angiography
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern or right axis deviation

differential.name: Asthma exacerbation
differential.why_considered: Cough, wheeze, and chest tightness are typical of reactive airway disease

history: Cough worse at night or with exercise and cold air

differential.name: Acute bronchitis
differential.why_considered: A cough lasting one to three weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection is the most common cause of acute cough

history: Cough may be dry or productive of clear to yellow sputum
No high fever or systemic toxicity
exam: Clear lungs or scattered rhonchi that clear with cough

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Reflux is a common cause of chronic cough, especially when it occurs at night or after meals

history: Cough worse after meals or when lying flat
labs: Trial of acid suppression may improve symptoms

differential.name: Post-nasal drip syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough from upper airway irritation is very common and often accompanies allergic rhinitis or sinusitis

exam: Visible posterior pharyngeal drip or cobblestoning

differential.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough is a hallmark of COPD in smokers

history: Chronic daily productive cough for months to years
imaging: Hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms on chest radiograph

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: A persistent or changing cough in a smoker can be the first sign of a lung tumor
differential.trigger: Cough lasting more than 8 weeks, hemoptysis, weight loss, or a changing cough in a long-term smoker

imaging: Lung mass, hilar adenopathy, or pleural effusion on chest imaging

differential.name: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor cough
differential.why_considered: A dry, persistent cough is a well-known side effect of ACE inhibitors

history: Current use of lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, or benazepril
Dry hacking cough starting weeks after starting the drug
labs: Cough resolves within weeks of stopping the medication

severity.mild: Acute cough with a clear cause such as a cold; patient is comfortable, afebrile, and eating and sleeping normally
severity.moderate: Cough is disruptive to sleep or work, with low-grade fever or chest discomfort but no respiratory distress
severity.severe: Cough with tachypnea, hypoxemia, or inability to speak in full sentences; requires urgent evaluation
severity.critical: Respiratory failure or shock from an underlying cause such as severe pneumonia or pulmonary embolism

red_flags.meaning: Suggests infection, malignancy, or pulmonary embolism; needs urgent workup

red_flags.finding: Shortness of breath at rest or hypoxemia
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or another serious lung process
Suggests bacterial pneumonia or another systemic infection

red_flags.finding: Unintentional weight loss or night sweats
Cough lasting more than 8 weeks despite treatment
red_flags.meaning: Requires evaluation for chronic causes including malignancy and reflux
Suggests upper airway obstruction or a deep neck infection

complications.name: Rib fracture from severe coughing
clues: Focal chest wall pain worse with movement

complications.name: Syncope with coughing
clues: Loss of consciousness immediately after a coughing paroxysm

special_populations.differences: Young children cannot describe their cough; parents report noisy breathing, poor feeding, or a barking cough. Cough medicines are not recommended under age 4.
May have a blunted fever response and a weaker cough reflex, so pneumonia can present with confusion or falls rather than prominent cough.
Cough is often from a viral illness or reflux, but shortness of breath and leg swelling should raise concern for a clot.
Can develop severe or unusual lung infections with minimal symptoms and a normal chest exam.

key_questions.question: How long have you had the cough?
key_questions.looking_for: Under 3 weeks suggests an acute cause such as a viral illness; over 8 weeks points to chronic causes like reflux, asthma, post-nasal drip, or ACE inhibitor use

key_questions.question: Did it start suddenly, and were you choking or eating just before?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset while eating or choking suggests aspiration of a foreign body

key_questions.question: Is the cough dry or are you bringing up phlegm? What color is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear to yellow sputum fits a viral illness; purulent or blood-streaked sputum raises concern for pneumonia or another lower airway process

key_questions.question: Have you coughed up any blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Hemoptysis suggests infection, malignancy, or pulmonary embolism and needs urgent workup

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath, and is it only with activity or also at rest?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea at rest or hypoxemia suggests pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or another serious lung process

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: High fever with shaking chills suggests bacterial pneumonia; night sweats and weight loss suggest tuberculosis or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss raises concern for tuberculosis or lung cancer

key_questions.question: What makes the cough better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse at night or with exercise and cold air suggests asthma; worse after meals or lying flat suggests reflux

key_questions.question: Do you have a runny or stuffy nose, post-nasal drip, or constant throat clearing?
key_questions.looking_for: Upper airway symptoms suggest post-nasal drip or allergic rhinitis as the driver of the cough

key_questions.question: Any heartburn or sour taste in your mouth?
key_questions.looking_for: Reflux symptoms point to gastroesophageal reflux disease as a chronic cough cause

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of asthma, allergies, or COPD?
key_questions.looking_for: Known reactive airway disease or COPD changes the pretest probability of an exacerbation

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood pressure medicines, especially lisinopril or another ACE inhibitor?
key_questions.looking_for: A dry cough starting weeks after an ACE inhibitor is a common reversible cause

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or did you smoke in the past? How much and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: A long smoking history raises concern for COPD and lung cancer, especially with a changing cough

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you been sick with a cold or flu recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent contact supports a viral upper respiratory infection as the cause

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent surgery, hospital stay, long travel, or immobility?
key_questions.looking_for: Venous thromboembolism risk factors raise concern for pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Any chest pain, especially when you take a deep breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Pleuritic chest pain suggests pneumonia or pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a cough like this before, and what turned out to be the cause?
key_questions.looking_for: A prior similar episode with a known cause can point to a recurrent process such as asthma or reflux

reasoning_points: Duration separates acute (under 3 weeks), subacute (3 to 8 weeks), and chronic (over 8 weeks) cough, which drives the differential
A preceding cold with clear to yellow sputum and no systemic toxicity fits acute bronchitis or a viral upper respiratory infection
Fever, tachypnea, focal crackles, or hypoxemia point to community-acquired pneumonia
Sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, pleuritic pain, or a clear chest exam despite marked breathlessness raise concern for pulmonary embolism
Nighttime or exercise-induced cough with wheezing suggests asthma
Post-nasal drip or allergic rhinitis is a common upper airway cause of chronic cough
Reflux symptoms or cough after meals and when lying flat suggest gastroesophageal reflux disease
A dry cough starting weeks after an ACE inhibitor is a reversible drug side effect
A long smoking history with a changing cough, hemoptysis, or weight loss raises concern for COPD or lung cancer
Red flags such as hemoptysis, resting dyspnea, weight loss, night sweats, or stridor require urgent evaluation

easy: Young adult with a recent cold, clear to yellow sputum, and no red flags
Clear lungs on exam and normal vital signs
medium: Cough lasting 3 to 8 weeks after a viral illness with persistent post-nasal drip
Adult with known asthma and nighttime cough responding to a bronchodilator
Patient on lisinopril with a new dry cough and a normal chest exam
hard: Older adult with a blunted fever response presenting with confusion or a fall rather than prominent cough
Smoker with a changing cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss suggesting lung cancer
Pregnant patient with cough, dyspnea, and leg swelling raising concern for pulmonary embolism
Immunocompromised patient with minimal symptoms but a severe lung infection
Toddler with a barking cough or noisy breathing that the parent cannot describe well
